analysis.one_liner: Repeals Medicaid, CHIP, and the ACA and replaces them with fixed block grants to states.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by Rep. Rokita and 50 Republican cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program — the government health programs covering low-income families, children, seniors in nursing homes, and people with disabilities — and replaced them with a single annual grant to each state, fixed at what the state's federal Medicaid and CHIP funding was in fiscal 2012 [S2] [S3]. It would also have repealed the Affordable Care Act in its entirety [S2] [S3]. Each state would decide for itself who counts as 'indigent' and what counts as a covered health service, and the bill explicitly states that no individual would have an entitlement to care [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers benefit from capping federal spending: instead of the open-ended federal match that grows automatically with enrollment and medical costs, each state would get a grant frozen at its fiscal 2012 federal Medicaid and CHIP funding for ten years [S3]. State governments gain wide discretion — they define who qualifies, they can divert up to 30% of the grant to other welfare programs like cash assistance and food assistance, and the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have no oversight authority [S3]. Because federal spending cuts of this size flow disproportionately to higher-income taxpayers, the main financial winners are the wealthiest households.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers, states, and high-income households

how_it_helps.text: Replaces Medicaid and CHIP with quarterly block grants to states, each set at 25% of the state's fiscal 2012 federal funding under those programs — freezing the federal contribution for fiscal years 2014 through 2023 [S2] [S3].
Repeals the Affordable Care Act, the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act, and Social Security Act titles XIX (Medicaid) and XXI (CHIP) [S2] [S3].

Lets states define who is 'indigent' and what 'health-care-related items and services' means for their own program, and bars federal officials, including the HHS Secretary, from supervising how states spend the money [S3].
Allows states to spend up to 30% of the grant on other welfare programs, including TANF cash assistance and food assistance under the Food and Nutrition Act [S3].
Bars federal and, in most cases, state funds used with the grant from paying for abortions, with exceptions for rape, incest, and danger of death [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 60 to 90 million Americans enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP — mostly children, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and nursing home residents — would lose their guaranteed right to coverage, since states could tighten eligibility, cut benefits, or pay providers less without any federal entitlement or floor [S2] [S3]. States and safety-net hospitals would absorb costs that grow past the frozen grant, especially during recessions when enrollment spikes [S3]. People buying coverage through the ACA's exchanges would lose their subsidies and protections when the ACA is repealed [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid and CHIP enrollees and safety-net hospitals

drawbacks.text: The grant is fixed at fiscal 2012 levels and does not grow with medical costs, population, or recessions; states may only set aside a 'rainy day fund' out of their own capped grant, so the cut deepens every year as health care costs rise [S3].

States — not federal law — would define who is 'indigent' and what services are covered, and the bill states no individual has an entitlement to care, removing the guaranteed floor Medicaid and CHIP provide [S3].
Repealing the ACA would end exchange subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with pre-existing conditions all at once [S2] [S3].

States would still have to pay emergency care for non-permanent residents but explicitly could not pay for organ transplant procedures for them, and the abortion funding restrictions extend to state funds used alongside the grant [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The flexibility states gain is real but small next to what they give up: an open-ended federal match that automatically absorbs enrollment growth and recessions becomes a frozen annual check, so every year of rising medical costs is a deeper cut in care for low-income families. Repealing the ACA on the same effective date compounds the loss of coverage. The bill is a straightforward large reduction in federal support for low-income health care, with the state-discretion language serving as its selling point.

outcome.mechanism: After being referred to eight House committees and then to subcommittees, the bill sat in committee with no hearing or vote and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Todd Rokita introduced the bill on February 6, 2013, joined by 50 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].

The same day, it was referred to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations — and over the following weeks to subcommittees on Health, Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Immigration and Border Security, and Health/Employment/Labor/Pensions [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or floor vote is recorded in its action history, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicaid and CHIP continued operating as guaranteed entitlements, the ACA remained in force, and the hospitals, nursing homes, and states that depend on Medicaid funding avoided a ten-year freeze in federal support. Low-income enrollees kept the coverage the bill would have replaced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, and providers relying on Medicaid

for.name: Rep. Todd Rokita
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 6, 2013 to replace Medicaid and CHIP with state block grants and repeal the ACA [S1] [S3] [S5].

for.name: 50 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; health jurisdiction over Medicaid and CHIP
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 6, 2013 and referred it to its Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed with no hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 113th House
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat supported it; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to measure the split [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Hospitals that treat large numbers of Medicaid patients would face frozen federal funding and more uninsured patients if enrollment shrinks, raising uncompensated care costs. Their financial interest in this bill ran alongside enrollees' interest in keeping coverage.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care providers
industries.note: Medicaid is the largest payer of long-term care; a grant that does not grow with costs would pressure states to cut nursing home rates or slots. Providers and the seniors they serve both lose under this bill.

States gain wide discretion, including shifting up to 30% of funds to other welfare programs and freedom from federal health agency oversight, but they absorb all cost growth above the frozen grant and could face 10%-plus penalties from audits [S3].

States could use grant funds to subsidize private insurance purchase through risk pools, a potential new revenue channel, but repealing the ACA eliminates exchange subsidies and mandates that drove insurers' enrollment growth [S3].
